title: Automaton

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Gift of Murtogh D. Guinness, 1976
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A tiny golden frog with green enamel on its body, shown against a plain background. It is a small jeweled toy-like object only a few centimeters long.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record (title, date, medium, culture, country, length, credit line, classification, tags, public-domain flag, image URLs) and the Met object page description of the frog's materials and movement

context: A tiny Swiss automaton made around 1820 in the form of a frog, about 6.2 cm long. According to the Met, it is made of gold and green enamel set with pearls, with ruby eyes, and a mechanism makes the legs jump and croak.

descriptions.k: This tiny frog is made of gold and green glass. Its eyes are red jewels. Inside is a secret machine. It makes the frog jump and croak! It is only as long as your finger. Can you see its legs?
descriptions.g12: This little golden frog is a jewel with a secret. Its body is covered in green enamel, and its eyes are red rubies. Inside is a tiny machine that makes the legs jump and a croak sound. It is only about six centimeters long. Why would someone make a jewel that moves?
descriptions.g35: This frog was made in Switzerland around 1820. It is an automaton, a small machine that moves by itself. The frog is made of gold with green enamel, a kind of colored glass fired onto metal, and it has ruby eyes and pearls. The Met says a mechanism makes its legs jump and croak. It is about 6.2 centimeters long. What details make it look like a real frog?
descriptions.g68: Swiss makers around 1820 were famous for tiny mechanisms, and this gold and enamel frog is a good example. It combines jewelry skills, such as enamel, pearls, diamond, and ruby, with clockwork that makes the legs jump and the frog croak. At only 6.2 centimeters long, it is a luxury toy for adults. How do the materials make the frog both lifelike and unreal?
descriptions.g910: This Swiss automaton of about 1820 is an example of how jewelry and mechanics merged into one object. Green enamel gives the frog its skin, pearls and ruby eyes add luxury, and a hidden mechanism lets the legs move and the frog croak. Such objects were meant to surprise and delight. Consider how the maker balances naturalism with preciousness, and what it means to turn an animal into a jewel.
descriptions.g1112: A frog is an unusual subject for a luxury object, which may be part of the pleasure: this Swiss automaton of about 1820 turns a humble animal into gold, enamel, ruby, and pearl, then adds a mechanism that makes it jump and croak. Whether its original owners saw it as a toy, a curiosity, or a display of technical skill is not documented. How does an object that is both lifelike and artificial reflect the period's fascination with mechanism, nature, and wealth?

teacherNote.context: A tiny Swiss automaton frog from about 1820. The Met describes gold and green enamel, pearls, and ruby eyes, with a mechanism that makes the legs jump and the frog croak. The photograph is a still image, so students must imagine the motion.
directions: Ask students to design a tiny moving animal and sketch how its mechanism might be hidden.
Discuss the difference between a toy, a jewel, and a scientific instrument.
Compare this frog with the lion clock in the archive and discuss how makers surprise viewers with movement.
